# Phase 20: session snapshots

Gap table item C1. A long-document chat pays its prefill once per session; since
[Phase 17](PHASE_17.md) that prefill goes into the tier, and [Phase 19](PHASE_19.md) showed a
session can go on for many turns. Resuming a saved session should cost a sequential disk read
instead of a prefill. Questions were fixed in `configs/phase20.yaml` before any run.

## What was built

- `lazykv/snapshot.py`: **save a tier as its host store already is.** A sealed block is immutable
  once it is on the host, so a snapshot is the host store in its native `[B, h, 2, bs, d]` layout
  (written from the pinned pool without a permute), plus the few tokens still on the GPU (the dense
  layers' KV and each tiered layer's unsealed tail) and the next-token logits. Sections are aligned
  to 4 KiB so the reader can bypass the OS page cache.
- **Restore goes through the same boundary as prefill.** Each tiered layer's KV is rebuilt on the GPU
  one layer at a time and handed to `TieredLayer`'s constructor, exactly as `tiered_prefill` hands it
  a freshly computed layer, so a restored tier is a tier built by prefill at that length. Only slot
  residency is not carried over; it decides what is fetched, never what is attended.
- `scripts/09_snapshot.py`, `scripts/analyze_phase20.py`. `tests/test_snapshot.py`: a restored tiny
  model continues bit-identically, buffered and unbuffered, with the split before and after a block
  seals; the int8 tier and foreign files are refused.

## The run

Llama-3.2-1B-Instruct, one NIAH prompt per context, the speed kernel, Quest-style tier at a
12.5% budget, 3 prefills
and 3 restores per context in one process. The snapshot was
written to the internal NVMe (C:) and every restore read it unbuffered, so the page cache the save had
just filled could not help.

### Question 1: cost

| Context | Tiered prefill (median, range) | Restore (median, range) | of which disk read | of which rebuild | Read rate | Speedup |
| --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 32,768 | 5.74 s (5.73–7.26) | 0.64 s (0.64–0.75) | 0.33 s | 0.29 s | 3.21 GB/s | 8.9× (7.6× worst pair) |
| 65,536 | 18.02 s (17.96–18.76) | 1.23 s (1.22–1.38) | 0.66 s | 0.56 s | 3.26 GB/s | 14.7× (13.0× worst pair) |
| 130,048 | 60.69 s (60.63–62.31) | 2.34 s (2.34–2.49) | 1.21 s | 1.13 s | 3.53 GB/s | 25.9× (24.4× worst pair) |

- **Resuming is 8.9× to 25.9×
  faster than prefilling again, and the gap grows with context.** Prefill is compute-bound and its
  attention grows with the square of the context; a restore moves each KV byte once and grows
  linearly. Even pairing the slowest restore with the fastest prefill, it is at least
  7.6× faster.
- **About half of a restore is not the disk.** The disk read runs at
  3.2–3.5 GB/s; the rest is
  the rebuild, which copies each layer to the GPU and back into the host store through the prefill
  boundary, and the read and rebuild run one after the other. Reading straight into the pinned pool and computing the metadata from it and
  overlapping the next layer's read with this layer's rebuild could remove most of it (an expectation, not measured). It was not built: the boundary reuse is what makes a restore provably a prefill.

### Questions 2 and 3: size and exactness

| Context | Session KV | Snapshot | Snapshot / KV | Save (first prefill) | State hash equal | Decoded tokens equal |
| --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: | --: |
| 32,768 | 1,024 MiB | 1,024 MiB | 1.0005 | 1.05 s (1.02 GB/s) | 3 / 3 | 3 / 3 |
| 65,536 | 2,048 MiB | 2,048 MiB | 1.0002 | 1.84 s (1.17 GB/s) | 3 / 3 | 2 / 3 |
| 130,048 | 4,064 MiB | 4,064 MiB | 1.0001 | 4.67 s (0.91 GB/s) | 3 / 3 | 2 / 3 |

- **A snapshot is the session's KV and nothing more:** at most
  1.0005× its bytes, the excess being alignment, the
  header and the logits.
- **Every restore is exact.** The full tier state hash matched the prefilled tier's on
  9 of 9 restores.
  The decoded tokens matched on 7 of
  9. With identical state, a token mismatch comes from the
  decode, not the snapshot: cuDNN's single-query kernel is not bit-repeatable (Phase 1), which is why the
  config named the state hash as the exactness check before the run.
- The NIAH score in `metrics.json` is the 1B model's at a 12.5% budget on the prefilled tier; it
  measures the model and the budget, not the snapshot, and is not a result of this phase.

## What this phase does not show

- One model, one prompt per context, one disk. A slower disk lowers the read rate and the speedup;
  the rebuild half does not depend on it.
- Save cost was measured once per context, after the first prefill; it is paid once per session and
  is not on the resume path.
- No session was resumed mid-conversation in this run; the unit tests cover a split after decoding,
  this run splits at the prefill boundary.
